demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it
I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay
Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.explanation: For trauma involving unexpected death of a loved one, repeated triggers centered on children (kids crying, being around children) are hard to explain unless the deceased was a child or the death specifically involved children; with no supporting memory, threat, or appraisal content linking the loss to children, this trigger pattern is clinically incoherent.

issues.item: Triggers: Children Present: Being around children
issues.explanation: Avoiding sex is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The reported triggers and appraisals focus on grief/disconnection rather than bodily violation, intimacy threat, or sexual trauma themes, so this strategy appears to address a symptom domain absent elsewhere in the selected items.

Feeling 'like an object, not like a person' is more characteristic of interpersonal violation, coercion, or depersonalized trauma responses. In a bereavement profile, without corroborating memory, trigger, or strategy content suggesting objectification or dissociation, this appraisal is difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Triggers: Children Present: Being around children
issues.explanation: For traumatic bereavement, 'being around children' is not impossible as a trigger, but in this profile it lacks support from the other selected items. There are no memory, threat, or appraisal items linking the loss to children or parenting, so this trigger feels clinically unanchored relative to the rest of the profile.

'Avoid Sex' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the self-report. Sexual avoidance is more typically anchored to interpersonal/sexual trauma or marked contamination/intimacy themes, none of which are represented elsewhere in the selected triggers or appraisals for a bereavement presentation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person
issues.explanation: 'I feel like an object, not like a person' is poorly matched to unexpected death of a loved one in the absence of other humiliation, assault, or depersonalization-related content. It does not cohere well with the grief-linked triggers and appears disconnected from the stated maladaptive strategies and formulation.

vignette:
# Clinical Vignette: María

María was thirty-eight when her brother Diego died. It happened on a Tuesday afternoon in March, sudden and without warning—a myocardial infarction while he was driving home from his construction job. He was forty-one. The police found him slumped against the steering wheel on the shoulder of Route 9, and the sirens that had wailed through the neighbourhood that day became, in her mind, the sound of the world breaking apart. She had not been there. She was at the factory where she had worked for sixteen years, operating a stamping press, when her sister-in-law's call came through. By the time María arrived at the hospital, Diego was already dead.

In the weeks that followed, María found herself unable to move forward. She replayed the last conversation she had had with Diego—a brief phone call two days before his death in which he had complained about traffic and asked if she wanted him to pick up groceries. She had said no, she was fine, she would shop herself. She went over that exchange again and again, searching for some sign she had missed, some moment where she might have detected something wrong in his voice, some way she could have prevented what came next. She knew, rationally, that a conversation about groceries held no predictive power, but the knowing did not stop her from turning it over in her mind during her shift, during her commute, late into the night. The details had become a kind of compulsion—she could not rest without examining them, as though understanding exactly how and why it happened might somehow unmake it.

What frightened María most was the possibility that she was fundamentally changed, that the person she had been before March was gone. She had come to believe that her life had been destroyed by Diego's death, that there was no trajectory forward that did not involve permanent misery. She used to laugh easily. She had had friends at the factory, women she would sit with at lunch and share gossip and complaints. Now, when one of them mentioned her own mother's recent illness or spoke about losing a cousin years ago, María would feel a tightness in her chest and an overwhelming need to leave the conversation. She began eating her lunch alone in her car. When her coworker Rosa asked if everything was okay, if she wanted to talk, María found herself asking Rosa repeatedly for reassurance—"Do you think I'm going to be okay? Do you think I'm handling this right?"—even as she was pulling away, even as she was making it clear through her distance that she did not want to be known.

She stopped attending family gatherings. Her mother had asked her to come to a quinceañera for a cousin, and María had said no, she couldn't, she just couldn't be around people celebrating. The thought of a funeral or cemetery visit was unbearable—she had not been to Diego's grave since the burial, and the idea of it, of standing in that place where his body lay, of seeing his name carved into stone, made her feel as though she might collapse. Even conversations about loss in the abstract became dangerous. When her supervisor mentioned that he had lost his father, María excused herself and spent twenty minutes in the bathroom stall, breathing unevenly, unable to return to the floor.

The sirens were everywhere. They came through the factory district regularly, and each time one passed—the wail building and then fading—María's body would jolt, her hands would shake, and she would have to step away from her machine. She had been written up twice for safety violations, for not wearing her protective gear properly because her concentration had fractured. Her supervisor had begun to watch her more closely, and she knew it was only a matter of time before her employment became precarious.

It was her mother who finally insisted she seek help. María had called her in tears one evening after hearing a siren and spending an hour unable to do anything but sit in the dark. Her mother, who had lost a son and was managing her own grief, said that María was suffering in a way that was beyond what either of them could fix alone. María agreed, though she did not believe that anything could truly help, that any therapist could restore what had been lost or make her feel as though she belonged to the world again. But she made the appointment, because her mother asked, because she was afraid of losing her job, because somewhere beneath the conviction that her life was destroyed lay a faint, terrified hope that she might be wrong.
